<description>
There is a fair amount of work going into the indices at the moment, and no cheap way to tell whether a change actually improves what it set out to improve: checking end to end means a full IBD. The only index benchmark in the tree, `BlockFilterIndexSync`, syncs coinbase-only blocks, so it cannot show anything that scales with what a block contains, and there is none at all for `TxIndex` or `TxoSpenderIndex`.

This adds shared helpers in `src/bench/index_sync_util.{h,cpp}` that build a chain of blocks with chained, validly-signed transactions (~2 inputs and ~2 outputs each, every output in a block paying a distinct key), and on top of them, for txindex, txospenderindex and blockfilterindex:

- `<Index>SyncDisk` / `<Index>SyncMem` — full sync with the index database on the filesystem, and in memory.
- `<Index>Lookup` — one query per indexed key (`FindTx`, `FindSpender`).

How far apart Disk and Mem land depends on the data directory, which defaults to a tmpfs on many Linux systems, where both variants write to RAM and report about the same number. Pointing `-testdatadir` at real storage makes Disk pay real writes. The index stays in LevelDB's write buffer at this chain size, so the difference is mostly the synced writes that create the database (Linux, btrfs on NVMe, default 50x50 chain, median of 3 runs):

| Benchmark                           | tmpfs (default) | btrfs via `-testdatadir` |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------: | -----------------------: |
| `TxIndexSyncDisk`                   |          6.1 ms |                  34.8 ms |
| `TxIndexSyncMem`                    |          5.4 ms |                   4.5 ms |
| `TxIndexLookup`                     |          5.9 us |                   5.9 us |
| `TxoSpenderIndexSyncDisk`           |          5.5 ms |                  36.7 ms |
| `TxoSpenderIndexSyncMem`            |          5.4 ms |                   5.4 ms |
| `TxoSpenderIndexLookup`             |          6.8 us |                   6.3 us |
| `BlockFilterIndexSyncRealisticDisk` |          8.4 ms |                  41.8 ms |
| `BlockFilterIndexSyncRealisticMem`  |          7.8 ms |                  15.6 ms |

The lookups have a single variant, and barely move between the two columns: the database answers them from the write buffer either way, and the block file they read lives in the data directory whatever `f_memory` says.

The Mem rows barely moving is the check that `MemEnv` really keeps the database off the filesystem. Blockfilter is the exception, because its filters go to the data directory through `m_filter_fileseq` whatever `f_memory` says, so both of its variants pay that write.

`BenchIndexSync()` also forces a chainstate flush, without which `BaseIndex::Commit()` returns early and the commit path stays out of the measurement.

The existing `BlockFilterIndexSync` is left untouched: it scales with the number of blocks over near-empty filters, the new one with what a block contains. The suite runs in about 15 s.

A last commit documents in `doc/benchmarking.md` how to measure syscalls, on-disk size and peak memory around `bench_bitcoin`, which nanobench does not report.

I have used this on those two pull requests, and in both the interesting number was one the existing benchmark could not produce: #35531 (5-byte siphash keys) trades a 49% smaller index on disk for a lookup regression that grows with index size, and #34489 (batch db writes) cuts `write` syscalls by 91% with CPU unchanged. The numbers are in those threads.

Disclosure: I used claude to help me in some parts, however all code has been verified by me and I ran the bench manually on the scenarios mentioned.
</description>
